meta.title: MAIA — Music Adversarial Inpainting
meta.description: MAIA research page: importance-driven music adversarial attacks, verified GACELA regeneration, paper evidence, and limitations.

hero.subtitle: Music Adversarial Inpainting Attack
hero.description: Locate influential musical regions, regenerate only those regions, and evaluate security impact together with perceptual quality.
hero.scope: Real GACELA output at fixed regions; no sample-level attack claim is inferred.

question.title: Can an MIR model be challenged without turning music into noise?
question.body: Conventional audio attacks often optimize imperceptible perturbations without respecting musical structure. MAIA asks whether a model's most influential regions can instead be regenerated with a learned music prior, preserving a coherent listening experience while exposing model vulnerability.
question.localizeBody: Find the time–frequency regions that contribute most to the target model's decision.
question.regenerateBody: Use a conditional generative inpainting model to replace bounded regions using their musical context.
question.evaluateBody: Measure model impact and audio quality together instead of treating either dimension in isolation.

threat.title: Two access settings, one bounded-edit principle
threat.whiteBody: Grad-CAM localizes influential regions. Reconstruction and untargeted attack losses guide GACELA for at most 10 optimization iterations, with loss weights selected from {0.5, 1.0, 2.0}.
threat.blackBody: A 0.5-second coarse-to-fine masking procedure estimates region importance. CMA-ES then searches GACELA's latent space under a 1,000-query budget.
threat.scope: The paper evaluates cover-song identification with CoverHunter on SHS100K and music-genre classification with IDS-NMR on GTZAN.

rationale.title: Change less, but change what matters
rationale.body: MAIA does not edit the whole waveform. It first ranks influential regions, then constrains generative changes to a small set of selected intervals. This makes the intervention interpretable in time and gives the inpainting model surrounding context for musically plausible reconstruction.

method.title: How MAIA Works
method.subtitle: A three-step importance-driven adversarial inpainting framework
method.step1Body: Identify critical time-frequency regions that most influence the model's decision
method.whiteBody: Use gradient-weighted class activation mapping on the target model's final-block representation.
method.blackBody: Rank masked chunks by loss change per unit duration, then refine the most influential chunk.
method.step2Body: Select the highest-ranked regions for bounded generative modification
method.priorityBody: Rank candidate regions by model-derived importance and retain the top regions under the edit budget.
method.refineBody: In the black-box setting, recursively split the highest-scoring coarse region to obtain finer localization.
method.step3Body: Reconstruct selected segments with GACELA and task-specific adversarial guidance
method.gacelaBody: A generative adversarial context encoder reconstructs missing music from the audio surrounding each selected region.
method.lossBody: Balance reconstruction fidelity and untargeted attack effectiveness through a weighted objective.
method.figure4BeforeAlt: Before inpainting, from the paper figure
method.figure4AfterAlt: After inpainting, from the paper figure
method.figure4Caption: The paper figure illustrates context-conditioned local music reconstruction.

demo.title: Real model-based regeneration at MAIA-selected regions
demo.disclaimer: This interactive example isolates the generative inpainting component of MAIA. The displayed audio is produced by an actual music inpainting model at the selected regions. Paper-level attack performance is reported separately and is not inferred from this individual example.
demo.locateBody: The highlighted centers preserve the three region positions used by the earlier MAIA page. They are provenance-preserved interface metadata, not a new target-model localization run.
demo.locateAlt: Original spectrogram with three selected regions
demo.regenerateBody: Each view uses the same 30-second time axis. GACELA's 32-frame checkpoint alignment is recorded in the manifest, and the original region centers are preserved.
demo.differenceAlt: Difference spectrogram calculated from the original and regenerated audio
demo.differenceCaption: Computed from the two WAV files. Changes outside the effective regions are zero in the validation output.
demo.listenBody: All three sources share one timeline. Switching tracks preserves the current position; region looping constrains playback to the selected interval.
demo.abToggleAria: Switch between original and regenerated audio at the same time
demo.regionAria: Choose a region for loop playback

evidence.title: Evidence and limitations
evidence.disclaimer: These values are aggregate results from Table 1 of the paper. They are not predictions or metrics for the interactive sample above.
evidence.tableCaption: Table 1 excerpt — MAIA rows reported for two tasks and two access settings
evidence.limit1Body: The paper studies two MIR tasks and two target system–dataset pairs; broader generalization requires additional targets and music domains.
evidence.limit2Body: White-box MAIA requires gradients and model access. Black-box MAIA relies on query feedback and uses up to 1,000 queries.
evidence.limit3Body: The public sample verifies GACELA-based local regeneration only. No target classifier, retrieval model, prediction, or attack-search loop was run for it.
evidence.evaluation: The paper evaluates ASR, post-attack mAP or accuracy, FAD using MERT-V0, LSD, and a five-point subjective listening study with 100 participants.

bridge.title: From Localized Music Attacks to Multimodal Agent Safety
bridge.subtitle: A methodological transfer, not an experimental result of MAIA.
bridge.a1: Identify high-risk observations, context, memory, or actions
bridge.a3: Perform gradient-based and query-based red teaming
bridge.m4: Measure attack effectiveness and perceptual quality together
bridge.a4: Evaluate security impact, task utility, side effects, and human perception
bridge.boundary: MAIA does not directly solve prompt injection, jailbreak, tool authorization, or trusted execution. The bridge identifies a transferable evaluation methodology: locate influential inputs, apply bounded counterfactual changes, and jointly measure attack effectiveness and utility preservation.
